title: The prince who stopped caring
hookLine: a prince comes home and stops caring about everything
carry: vairagya: honest doubt is where wisdom starts
tomorrow: is your life already written? two rams in a field answer.

lines: A PRINCE ASKS WHAT IT'S ALL FOR.
cards: Some people come back from a big trip and can't settle. The bedroom looks smaller. The old routine feels flat.
Friends ask how it was, and the answer won't fit in a text. Long ago a prince came home like that. Rama returns from a pilgrimage, and something in him has gone quiet.
He grows thin, sits alone, and stops caring for the things princes care for. Then a sage arrives at court, and Rama is called in. He doesn't talk about duty.
He asks what any of it is for.

teach.b: That question opens the Yoga Vasistha, a long conversation between Rama and his teacher, Vasistha. Rama speaks to the court, and it isn't polite. Wealth comes and goes, he says.
Youth fades. The body wears out. Pleasures leave a person thirstier than before.
He can't see what's worth holding on to.

teach.h: VAIRAGYA: NO APPETITE FOR THE PRIZES.
teach.b: The book's first section is named for this mood: vairagya, dispassion, the loss of appetite for the world's prizes. Here's the surprise.
Nobody in the court scolds him. Nobody tells him to cheer up and get back to work. The sages hear his questions as the start of wisdom, a sign that he's ready to be taught.

So Vasistha, the family's own teacher, begins. The rest of the book is his answer, with stories inside stories, and this path reads it in selections over the coming days. Notice where it catches Rama.

teach.h: AN HONEST QUESTION IS A DOOR.
teach.b: Not as the hero who wins his wife back from Lanka, but earlier, a young man in a palace, asking honest, uncomfortable questions out loud. The book treats those questions not as a problem to fix, but as a door.

how: The Yoga Vasistha is read in Advaita Vedanta circles and by students of yoga philosophy; readers often meet it through abridgments and selections rather than the whole.

o: an epic of Rama's battle to win back his wife
a book of stretches and poses named for an old sage
a long talk where a sage answers a young prince's doubts

games.q: who's who at court — tap the pairs.
p: the prince who comes home and goes quiet
dispassion: no appetite for the prizes
hear his questions as a door

s: the Yoga Vasistha opens with Rama winning a battle
it opens earlier, with a young prince at home asking what any of it is for.
in the book, the sages welcome Rama's questions as the start of wisdom
nobody scolds him; they treat his doubts as readiness to be taught.
it's dispassion: losing the appetite for the world's prizes.

games.q: a coworker who's usually upbeat says lately none of the job feels worth it. the manager's instinct is a pep talk. what would the court in the Yoga Vasistha do?
o: hear the question out, and take it seriously.
tell him to cheer up and get back to work.
tell him to quit everything and go away.
games.why: nobody scolds Rama or hurries him back to work. the sages hear his honest question as the start of wisdom, and a teacher begins to answer.

practice: If you can, get up and walk slowly through the room you're in, or one nearby, for about a minute. Let your eyes land on things you've stopped seeing: a shelf, a photo, a mug.
Don't try to feel anything about them; just notice what's there, then sit back down for the rest of the time.

wordCard.voice: The Yoga Vasistha: Rama's questions, and his teacher Vasistha's long answer, read here in selections.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the book's name, tied to Vasistha, the teacher who answers Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: vairagya, a prince's honest doubt, is where wisdom starts. Sixteen-oh-one, done.

sources.ref: Yoga Vasistha, Vairagya Prakarana (Rama's return from pilgrimage and withdrawal; Vishvamitra's visit to Dasharatha; Rama's speech on the impermanence of wealth, youth and the body; the sages' response)
